Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake
text:
2.1 Data Source
The primary data source is the Address-Based Population Registration System (ADNKS), published annually by TurkStat (TÜİK). ADNKS is an administrative database that records the residential addresses of all individuals registered in Turkey, providing reliable and comprehensive population figures at the provincial level.
Source: TurkStat ADNKS, 2023
URL: data.tuik.gov.tr
RData file: deprem_goc.RData

title: Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake

2.2 General Information About Data
The dataset covers the 11 provinces directly affected by the February 6, 2023 earthquakes: Kahramanmaraş, Hatay, Adıyaman, Malatya, Gaziantep, Şanlıurfa, Diyarbakır, Kilis, Osmaniye, Adana, and Elazığ.
Each observation corresponds to one province and includes the following variables:

title: Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake
text:
2.3 Reason of Choice
This dataset is publicly available, regularly updated, and directly published by TurkStat, ensuring reliability. Also, the 2022 and 2023 editions capture the population status immediately before and after the earthquakes, making it ideal for measuring the demographic impact. Additionally, the provincial level of granularity is well-suited for comparative analysis across the affected region.
The February 6 earthquakes represent a critical turning point in Turkey’s demographic landscape. Studying their impact on population movement contributes to our understanding of how large-scale disasters reshape human geography.

title: Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake
text:
2.4 Preprocessing
The raw data was downloaded from TurkStat in Excel format. The following preprocessing steps were applied:

Column selection: Only the province name, population and annual growth rate columns were retained.
Province filtering: The dataset was filtered to include only the 11 earthquake-affected provinces.
Type conversion: Population figures contained spaces as thousand separators and were converted to numeric format.
Derived variable: A population change variable (pop_change) was computed as the difference between 2023 and 2022 populations.

library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)

earthquake_provinces <- c("Kahramanmaraş", "Hatay", "Adıyaman",
                          "Malatya", "Gaziantep", "Şanlıurfa",
                          "Diyarbakır", "Kilis", "Osmaniye",
                          "Adana", "Elazığ")

df_raw <- read_excel("adnks_il.xls", skip = 2)

df <- df_raw |>
  rename(
    province      = 1,
    population_22 = 2,
    population_23 = 3,
    growth_rate   = 10
  ) |>
  select(province, population_22, population_23, growth_rate) |>
  filter(province %in% earthquake_provinces) |>
  mutate(
    population_22 = as.numeric(gsub(" ", "", population_22)),
    population_23 = as.numeric(gsub(" ", "", population_23)),
    growth_rate   = as.numeric(growth_rate),
    pop_change    = population_23 - population_22
  )

save(df, file = "deprem_goc.RData")

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(stringi)
library(htmltools)
library(scales)
library(htmlwidgets)

normalize_city <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    str_to_upper(locale = "tr") %>%
    stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") %>%
    str_trim()
}

geo_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alpers/Turkey-Maps-GeoJSON/master/tr-cities.json"

tr_map <- st_read(geo_url, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(city_key = normalize_city(name))

eq_provinces <- c(
  "ADANA", "ADIYAMAN", "DIYARBAKIR", "ELAZIG", "GAZIANTEP",
  "HATAY", "KAHRAMANMARAS", "KILIS", "MALATYA", "OSMANIYE", "SANLIURFA"
)

selected_destinations <- c(
  "ISTANBUL", "ANKARA", "MERSIN", "ANTALYA", "IZMIR",
  "KONYA", "KAYSERI", "MARDIN"
)

city_coords <- tribble(
  ~city_key, ~city_label, ~lat, ~lng,
  "ADANA", "Adana", 37.00, 35.32,
  "ADIYAMAN", "Adıyaman", 37.76, 38.28,
  "DIYARBAKIR", "Diyarbakır", 37.91, 40.22,
  "ELAZIG", "Elazığ", 38.67, 39.22,
  "GAZIANTEP", "Gaziantep", 37.07, 37.38,
  "HATAY", "Hatay", 36.20, 36.16,
  "KAHRAMANMARAS", "Kahramanmaraş", 37.58, 36.92,
  "KILIS", "Kilis", 36.72, 37.12,
  "MALATYA", "Malatya", 38.35, 38.31,
  "OSMANIYE", "Osmaniye", 37.07, 36.25,
  "SANLIURFA", "Şanlıurfa", 37.16, 38.80,
  "ANKARA", "Ankara", 39.93, 32.86,
  "ISTANBUL", "İstanbul", 41.02, 28.97,
  "MERSIN", "Mersin", 36.80, 34.64,
  "ANTALYA", "Antalya", 36.90, 30.70,
  "IZMIR", "İzmir", 38.42, 27.14,
  "KONYA", "Konya", 37.87, 32.48,
  "KAYSERI", "Kayseri", 38.72, 35.49,
  "MARDIN", "Mardin", 37.31, 40.74
)

damage <- tribble(
  ~Il, ~heavy, ~medium, ~light,
  "Adana", 2952, 11768, 71072,
  "Adıyaman", 56256, 18715, 72729,
  "Diyarbakır", 8602, 11209, 113223,
  "Elazığ", 10156, 15220, 31151,
  "Gaziantep", 29155, 20251, 236497,
  "Kahramanmaraş", 99326, 17887, 161137,
  "Malatya", 71519, 12801, 107765,
  "Hatay", 215255, 25957, 189317,
  "Kilis", 2514, 1303, 27969,
  "Osmaniye", 16111, 4122, 69466,
  "Şanlıurfa", 6163, 6041, 199401
) %>%
  mutate(city_key = normalize_city(Il),
         total_damage = heavy + medium + light)

pop_2022 <- read_excel("tr_nufus.xlsx") %>%
  rename(Yil = 1, Il = 2, Toplam = 3, Erkek = 4, Kadin = 5) %>%
  filter(Yil == 2022) %>%
  transmute(city_key = normalize_city(Il), pop_2022 = Toplam)

damage <- damage %>%
  left_join(pop_2022, by = "city_key") %>%
  mutate(
    heavy_per_1000 = heavy / pop_2022 * 1000,
    total_damage_per_1000 = total_damage / pop_2022 * 1000
  )

tr_map_damage <- tr_map %>%
  left_join(damage, by = "city_key")

damage_pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "YlOrRd",
  domain = tr_map_damage$heavy_per_1000,
  na.color = "#eeeeee"
)

migration <- read_excel("deprem_goc_ham_filtreli.xlsx", skip = 2) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  filter(!is.na(yil)) %>%
  mutate(
    yil = as.integer(yil),
    from_key = normalize_city(goc_veren_il_adi),
    to_key = normalize_city(goc_alan_il_adi)
  )

flows <- migration %>%
  filter(yil == 2023,
         from_key %in% eq_provinces,
         to_key %in% selected_destinations) %>%
  group_by(from_key, to_key) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(aldigi_goc, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(city_coords, by = c("from_key" = "city_key")) %>%
  rename(from_label = city_label, from_lat = lat, from_lng = lng) %>%
  left_join(city_coords, by = c("to_key" = "city_key")) %>%
  rename(to_label = city_label, to_lat = lat, to_lng = lng) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from_lat), !is.na(to_lat)) %>%
  mutate(
    origin_group = from_label,
    flow_group = paste0("flow_", from_label),
    origin_marker_group = paste0("origin_", from_label),
    dest_group = paste0("dest_", from_label),
    line_weight = rescale(value, to = c(3, 12)),
    line_opacity = rescale(value, to = c(0.55, 1)),
    popup_text = paste0(
      "<b>", from_label, " → ", to_label, "</b><br>",
      "Migration volume: ", format(value, big.mark = ","), " people"
    )
  )

origin_points <- flows %>%
  group_by(origin_group, origin_marker_group, from_label, from_lat, from_lng) %>%
  summarise(total_outflow = sum(value), .groups = "drop")

destination_all <- flows %>%
  group_by(to_key, to_label, to_lat, to_lng) %>%
  summarise(total_inflow = sum(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(dest_group = "dest_ALL")

destination_by_origin <- flows %>%
  group_by(origin_group, dest_group, to_key, to_label, to_lat, to_lng) %>%
  summarise(total_inflow = sum(value), .groups = "drop")

destination_points <- bind_rows(destination_all, destination_by_origin) %>%
  mutate(radius = rescale(total_inflow, to = c(6, 20)))

origin_icon <- awesomeIcons(
  icon = "home",
  iconColor = "white",
  markerColor = "red",
  library = "fa"
)

m <- leaflet(
  options = leafletOptions(
    zoomControl = FALSE,
    dragging = FALSE,
    scrollWheelZoom = FALSE,
    doubleClickZoom = FALSE,
    boxZoom = FALSE,
    touchZoom = FALSE
  )
) %>%
  addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") %>%
  setView(lng = 36.5, lat = 38.0, zoom = 6) %>%
  addPolygons(
    data = tr_map_damage,
    fillColor = ~damage_pal(heavy_per_1000),
    fillOpacity = ~ifelse(is.na(heavy_per_1000), 0.10, 0.80),
    color = "white",
    weight = 0.8,
    popup = ~ifelse(
      is.na(heavy_per_1000),
      paste0("<b>", name, "</b><br>Not included in earthquake damage dataset."),
      paste0(
        "<b>", Il, "</b><br>",
        "Heavy / collapsed housing: ", format(heavy, big.mark = ","), "<br>",
        "Heavy damage per 1,000 residents: ", round(heavy_per_1000, 1), "<br>",
        "Total damage per 1,000 residents: ", round(total_damage_per_1000, 1)
      )
    )
  )

for (i in seq_len(nrow(flows))) {
  m <- m %>%
    addPolylines(
      lng = c(flows$from_lng[i], flows$to_lng[i]),
      lat = c(flows$from_lat[i], flows$to_lat[i]),
      color = "#9b111e",
      weight = flows$line_weight[i],
      opacity = flows$line_opacity[i],
      group = flows$flow_group[i],
      popup = flows$popup_text[i],
      label = paste0(
        flows$from_label[i], " → ", flows$to_label[i],
        ": ", format(flows$value[i], big.mark = ","), " people"
      )
    )
}

for (i in seq_len(nrow(origin_points))) {
  m <- m %>%
    addAwesomeMarkers(
      lng = origin_points$from_lng[i],
      lat = origin_points$from_lat[i],
      icon = origin_icon,
      group = origin_points$origin_marker_group[i],
      popup = paste0(
        "<b>", origin_points$from_label[i], "</b><br>",
        "Total outflow to selected destinations: ",
        format(origin_points$total_outflow[i], big.mark = ","), " people"
      ),
      label = origin_points$from_label[i]
    )
}

for (g in unique(destination_points$dest_group)) {
  m <- m %>%
    addCircleMarkers(
      data = destination_points %>% filter(dest_group == g),
      lng = ~to_lng,
      lat = ~to_lat,
      radius = ~radius,
      color = "#1a5276",
      fillColor = "#1a5276",
      fillOpacity = 0.78,
      weight = 1,
      group = g,
      popup = ~paste0(
        "<b>", to_label, "</b><br>",
        "Inflow: ", format(total_inflow, big.mark = ","), " people"
      ),
      label = ~paste0(to_label, ": ", format(total_inflow, big.mark = ","), " people")
    )
}

m <- m %>%
  addLegend(
    position = "bottomright",
    pal = damage_pal,
    values = tr_map_damage$heavy_per_1000,
    title = HTML("Heavy damage<br>per 1,000 residents"),
    opacity = 0.8
  ) %>%
  addControl(
    html = HTML(
      paste0(
        "<div style='background:white;padding:8px 10px;border-radius:8px;",
        "box-shadow:0 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,.2);font-size:13px;'>",
        "<b>Filter by origin:</b><br>",
        "<select id='province_filter' style='margin-top:5px;width:190px;'>",
        "<option value='ALL'>All provinces</option>",
        paste0(
          "<option value='", sort(unique(flows$origin_group)), "'>",
          sort(unique(flows$origin_group)),
          "</option>",
          collapse = ""
        ),
        "</select></div>"
      )
    ),
    position = "topright"
  ) %>%
  addControl(
    html = HTML(
      "<div style='background:white;padding:8px 10px;border-radius:8px;
      box-shadow:0 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,.2);font-size:12px;'>
      <b>Flow layer</b><br>
      <span style='color:#9b111e;font-weight:bold;'>━</span> Line width/darkness = migration volume<br>
      <span style='color:#1a5276;font-weight:bold;'>●</span> Circle size = inflow volume
      </div>"
    ),
    position = "bottomleft"
  )

htmlwidgets::onRender(
  m,
  "
  function(el, x) {
    var map = this;

    function showGroup(originName) {
      map.eachLayer(function(layer) {
        if (layer.options && layer.options.group) {
          var g = layer.options.group;

          if (g.startsWith('flow_') || g.startsWith('origin_') || g.startsWith('dest_')) {
            if (originName === 'ALL') {
              if (g.startsWith('flow_') || g === 'dest_ALL') {
                if (!map.hasLayer(layer)) map.addLayer(layer);
              } else {
                if (map.hasLayer(layer)) map.removeLayer(layer);
              }
            } else {
              if (g === 'flow_' + originName || g === 'origin_' + originName || g === 'dest_' + originName) {
                if (!map.hasLayer(layer)) map.addLayer(layer);
              } else {
                if (map.hasLayer(layer)) map.removeLayer(layer);
              }
            }
          }
        }
      });
    }

    showGroup('ALL');

    var selector = document.getElementById('province_filter');
    if (selector) {
      selector.addEventListener('change', function() {
        showGroup(this.value);
      });
    }
  }
  "
)

(a) Video Summary
Video link: Veri Bilimi ve Endüstri Mühendisliği Üzerine Sohbetler – Mustafa Baydoğan & Erdi Daşdemir
In this video, Mustafa Baydoğan talks about the relationship between data science and industrial engineering and how data analysis methods are used to solve real-world problems. He explains that industrial engineers already work with tools like optimization, modeling, and system analysis, which are also essential in data science.
One of the main ideas in the talk is that before using machine learning or other data science techniques, it is important to first understand the real system and the problem itself. If the problem is not clearly defined, even very advanced models may give results that are not meaningful. Industrial engineers approach problems by analyzing the system, identifying key variables, and then building models that reflect the real situation.
The speaker also highlights real-world applications such as inventory management, demand forecasting in energy, e-commerce recommendation systems, and image-based predictions in manufacturing. These examples demonstrate that data science is not just about prediction but about supporting actionable decisions.
Another topic discussed in the video is the difference between traditional machine learning models and deep learning methods. Deep learning is especially useful when working with complex data like images, text, or audio. However, in many business problems, simpler and interpretable models are preferred because they are easier to understand and explain.
Overall, industrial engineers have an advantage in data science due to their ability to analyze systems, extract meaningful variables, and turn data into actionable decisions.

Why is it important to understand the real system before applying machine learning or data science methods?

Answer: Understanding the system helps identify the real cause of the problem and the important variables. If we directly apply machine learning without understanding the problem, the model may find patterns in the data but those patterns might not represent the real situation. When the problem is clearly understood, data science methods can be used more effectively.

According to the speaker, why are simpler and interpretable models often preferred in many business applications?


Because they always give the most accurate results
Because they need very large datasets
Because decision makers need to understand the model results
Because they only work with structured data

title: Population Movements After the February 6, 2023 Earthquake
text:
1. Project Overview and Scope
The February 6, 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes, with magnitudes of 7.7 and 7.6, are among the deadliest natural disasters in Turkey’s modern history. The disaster caused widespread destruction across 11 provinces, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and triggering one of the largest internal migration movements the country has ever seen.
This project analyzes the demographic impact of the earthquakes by examining population changes in the affected provinces before and after the disaster. Using TurkStat’s Address-Based Population Registration System (ADNKS), the study investigates how the earthquakes reshaped population distribution across Turkey.
Research questions:

How did the populations of the 11 affected provinces change between 2022 and 2023?
Which provinces experienced the greatest population loss?
Is there a relationship between earthquake damage intensity and population decline?

Objectives:

Quantify the population loss in earthquake-affected provinces
Identify migration patterns following the disaster
Visualize the demographic impact through maps and charts

Figure 1: Population trend in 11 earthquake provinces, 2018–2025. The vertical dashed line marks the February 6, 2023 earthquake. Hatay, Malatya and Kahramanmaraş show the sharpest discontinuities.





Between 2018 and 2022, all 11 provinces followed a stable upward trend. The earthquake broke that trend sharply in 2023. Hatay lost 141,000 residents (−8.4%), Malatya 70,000 (−8.6%), and Kahramanmaraş 61,000 (−5.2%) — losses with no peacetime precedent in Turkey’s modern history. Diyarbakır, Gaziantep and Şanlıurfa were barely touched, reflecting the uneven geography of destruction.

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
library(stringi)

normalize_city <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    stringr::str_to_upper(locale = "tr") %>%
    stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") %>%
    stringr::str_trim()
}

population <- read_excel("tr_nufus.xlsx") %>%
  rename(
    year = 1,
    province = 2,
    population = 3,
    male = 4,
    female = 5
  ) %>%
  mutate(city_key = normalize_city(province))

eq_provinces <- c(
  "KAHRAMANMARAS", "HATAY", "ADIYAMAN", "MALATYA",
  "GAZIANTEP", "SANLIURFA", "DIYARBAKIR", "KILIS",
  "OSMANIYE", "ADANA", "ELAZIG"
)

population_eq <- population %>%
  filter(city_key %in% eq_provinces)

recovery <- population_eq %>%
  group_by(city_key, province) %>%
  summarise(
    expected_2025 = predict(
      lm(population ~ year, data = cur_data() %>% filter(year <= 2022)),
      newdata = data.frame(year = 2025)
    ),
    actual_2025 = population[year == 2025],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    recovery_gap_pct = (actual_2025 - expected_2025) / expected_2025 * 100,
    status = case_when(
      recovery_gap_pct >= 0 ~ "Above expected trend",
      recovery_gap_pct >= -5 ~ "Near recovery",
      TRUE ~ "Still below trend"

    label = paste0(round(recovery_gap_pct, 1), "%")

  recovery,

  geom_vline(

    size = 3.7,

    x = "Gap from expected 2025 population",

Figure 3: Each province’s contribution to Turkey’s total GDP growth (percentage points, chain-linked volume index, base year 2009). Negative values mean the province dragged down overall growth. The 2023 values are paradoxically not catastrophic for some hard-hit provinces — emergency spending, debris removal, and reconstruction counted as economic activity. The 2024 rebound is driven largely by the construction sector.





A key paradox emerges from the GDP data: Hatay’s 2023 GDP contribution was positive (+0.093 pp) despite losing 141,000 residents. This is a well-known feature of national accounting — emergency relief, debris clearance, and international aid all register as economic activity regardless of welfare implications. The 2024 surge in Hatay (+0.165 pp), Kahramanmaraş (+0.113 pp) and Adiyaman (+0.110 pp) is primarily reconstruction-driven, raising the question of whether organic economic capacity will recover once rebuilding is complete.

The data allows a clear, data-driven answer to the public perception question:
Yes, the perception is largely correct — 2023 did bring an extraordinary migration wave into Ankara. Net migration from earthquake provinces surged to 43,962, compared to an annual average of 7,050 in the five preceding years. This is a fivefold increase, and Ankara received more net migrants from earthquake zones than any other province in Turkey that year.
However, the perception that “they are still here” is not well supported. By 2024, net migration from earthquake provinces to Ankara collapsed to 4,720 — near the pre-earthquake baseline. In 2025 it remained similarly low at 5,399. This means one of two things happened to the 2023 cohort: they either returned to their home provinces, or — more likely for a portion — they resettled in Ankara permanently and are no longer counted as “movers.” The net flow data cannot distinguish between these two outcomes.
What the data does rule out is a continuing large-scale influx. The shock was real, it was acute, and it resolved within 12 months in terms of flow magnitude.

In 2023, the red component spiked to +43,962 while the blue collapsed to −20,002 — two shocks that almost cancelled each other out. Earthquake-province arrivals surged to +43,962 net in 2023 — five times the 2018–2022 average. But Ankara’s total net migration was only 23,960, below the pre-earthquake average of 18,240. As people poured in from the south, Ankara simultaneously sent more people outward to other cities. The net result was unremarkable. What changed was the composition, not the size.

    fillOpacity = ~ifelse(is.na(heavy_per_1000), 0.12, 0.78),

    data = earthquake_centers,
    lng = ~lng,
    lat = ~lat,
    icon = quake_icon,
    label = ~paste0(location, " | Mw ", magnitude),

text:
1.1 Population trend in 11 earthquake provinces, 2018–2025
The earthquake created a clear break in the population trend of the most affected provinces. Hatay, Malatya, and Kahramanmaraş show the strongest discontinuities.


Show code
panel |>
  mutate(label = PROVINCE_LABELS[province]) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, total / 1e6,
             colour = province, group = province)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2023,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "red", alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 2023.1, y = 0.2,
           label = "2023 Earthquake",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "red") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COLORS, labels = PROVINCE_LABELS) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2018:2025) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Population (millions)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position  = "right",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








Figure 1: Population trend in 11 earthquake provinces, 2018–2025. The vertical dashed line marks the February 6, 2023 earthquake. Hatay, Malatya and Kahramanmaraş show the sharpest discontinuities.





Between 2018 and 2022, all 11 provinces followed a stable upward trend. The earthquake broke that trend sharply in 2023. Hatay lost 141,000 residents (−8.4%), Malatya 70,000 (−8.6%), and Kahramanmaraş 61,000 (−5.2%) — losses with no peacetime precedent in Turkey’s modern history. Diyarbakır, Gaziantep and Şanlıurfa were barely touched, reflecting the uneven geography of destruction.

3.1 Damage Intensity
This map illustrates the extent of damage caused by earthquakes in the region across the affected provinces. The 11 earthquake-affected provinces are color-coded based on the number of heavy/collapsed housing per 1,000 people. The darker the color of a province, the more severe the damage relative to its population. Hatay, which experienced the most severe destruction, is shown in a dark shade, with a heavy/destroyed housing density of 127.7 per 1,000 people. The provinces with the next highest levels of damage are Adıyaman at 88.6, Malatya at 88.0, and Kahramanmaraş at 84.4. The graph below shows the total population change in the 11 earthquake-affected provinces between 2018 and 2025. This graph indicates that the earthquake-affected provinces are still in the process of demographic recovery.

text:
4.5 Recovery Status by 2025



Show code
recovery <- pop |>
  group_by(province, label) |>
  group_modify(~{
    fit <- lm(total ~ year, data = .x |> filter(year <= 2022))
    tibble(
      expected_2025 = as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = tibble(year = 2025))),
      actual_2025 = .x$total[.x$year == 2025]
    )
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    recovery_gap_pct = (actual_2025 - expected_2025) / expected_2025 * 100,
    status = case_when(
      recovery_gap_pct >= 0 ~ "Above expected trend",
      recovery_gap_pct >= -5 ~ "Near recovery",
      TRUE ~ "Still below trend"
    )
  )

ggplot(recovery, aes(recovery_gap_pct, reorder(label, recovery_gap_pct), fill = status)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(recovery_gap_pct, 1), "%")),
    hjust = ifelse(recovery$recovery_gap_pct >= 0, -0.2, 1.15),
    size = 3.6,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Still below trend" = "#c0392b",
    "Near recovery" = "#f39c12",
    "Above expected trend" = "#27ae60"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.15, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Recovery Gap of Earthquake-Affected Provinces in 2025",
    subtitle = "Actual 2025 population compared with expected trend based on 2018–2022",
    x = "Gap from expected 2025 population",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Recovery status",
    caption = "0% = expected trend level. Negative values indicate remaining demographic deficit."
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

5.1 Gender-Based Population Change



Show code
gender_change <- pop |>
  filter(year %in% c(2022, 2023)) |>
  select(label, province, year, male, female) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = c(male, female), names_sep = "_") |>
  mutate(
    male_change_pct = (male_2023 - male_2022) / male_2022 * 100,
    female_change_pct = (female_2023 - female_2022) / female_2022 * 100,
    loss_intensity = (abs(male_change_pct) + abs(female_change_pct)) / 2
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(loss_intensity)) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = label)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(male_change_pct, female_change_pct),
    names_to = "gender",
    values_to = "change_pct"
  ) |>
  mutate(gender = recode(gender, male_change_pct = "Male", female_change_pct = "Female"))

ggplot(gender_change, aes(label, change_pct, fill = gender)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray35") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(change_pct, 1), "%")),
    position = position_dodge(0.75),
    vjust = ifelse(gender_change$change_pct < 0, 1.25, -0.35),
    size = 3,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Male" = "#1f77b4", "Female" = "#c51b7d")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.18, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Male and Female Population Change After the Earthquake",
    subtitle = "2022–2023 population change rates in earthquake-affected provinces",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Population change",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Negative values indicate population loss. This is an indirect demographic comparison, not direct gender-specific migration data."
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",

6.1 Ankara Migration Question
Ankara is examined in a separate section as it is one of the major cities to which migration from earthquake zones is most directed. Since looking only at net migration figures can be misleading, in this analysis, incoming and outgoing flows are evaluated together; the component from earthquake provinces and the component from other provinces are separated, and the structural change in Ankara’s migration dynamics is revealed more clearly.
The chart below breaks Ankara’s net migration into two components to isolate how much of the 2023 surge came specifically from earthquake-affected provinces, as opposed to broader population movements already underway.


Show code
ankara |>
  select(year, `From earthquake provinces` = net_eq, `From other provinces` = net_non_eq) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "component", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(year), value, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_line(
    data = ankara,
    aes(x = factor(year), y = net_total, group = 1),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = ankara,
    aes(x = factor(year), y = net_total),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "black",
    size = 2.6
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline_total, linetype = "dashed", color = "#264653") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "From earthquake provinces" = "#c0392b",
    "From other provinces" = "#457b9d"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Ankara Net Migration Decomposition",
    subtitle = "Earthquake-province component compared with all other provincial flows",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Net migration",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Bars show components. Black line shows total net migration. Dashed line shows 2018–2022 average total net migration."
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )





Ankara’s net migration from earthquake provinces and other provinces, 2018–2025.
